items.title: U.S. Midterm Elections and Policy Implications
points: Midterm elections occur Tuesday, November 4, 2026, determining control of Congress.

Republicans currently hold a narrow House majority (5-seat advantage) and Senate lead (53-47); polling suggests Democrats have a strong chance of taking the House, with the Senate remaining competitive.
A shift in congressional control could affect fiscal policy, regulation, and sectors including banks, crypto, defense, and healthcare.

items.title: October Jobs Report Expected Friday
points: October jobs report due Friday is expected to show 65K new jobs added, up from 29K in September.
Jobless rate is expected to stay at 4.2%, signaling a labor market that remains resilient but is moderating.
The report coincides with Moderna's earnings, but jobs data will dominate market attention.

items.title: Heavy Earnings Week Ahead
points: Monday: Apple reports its first earnings under new CEO John Ternus (succeeding prior leadership), with investors watching Apple Intelligence adoption and supply constraints; Palantir also reports.
Tuesday: AMD, Amgen, Pfizer, and Block report, with AMD closely watched for AI infrastructure spending trends.
Wednesday: Arm, Qualcomm, McDonald's, and Uber report, with the semiconductor names seen as key gauges of AI hardware demand.
Friday: Moderna reports alongside the October jobs data release.

items.title: Semiconductor Sector Downgraded on AI Spending Sustainability Concerns
points: Analyst Julian Lin downgrades semiconductor stocks to Sell despite recent price declines, citing rising interest rates, increasing debt costs, and customer concentration risk.
AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic have not yet established consistent profitability, raising doubts about reaching a projected $2.5–3 trillion in annual AI revenue by 2030.
Concerns include declining AI model prices, competition from cheaper alternatives, and doubts about sustainable enterprise spending on AI services.
Lin exited NVIDIA from his 'Best of Breed Growth Stocks' portfolio, arguing strong AI technology doesn't guarantee attractive investor returns.

items.title: Beaten-Down Tech Bonds Called Attractive
points: BofA strategist Michael Hartnett describes beaten-down tech bonds (corporate debt issued by technology companies that has fallen in price) as 'diamonds in the rough' due to more attractive valuations despite sector headwinds.

items.title: Brooks Running Thrives Under Berkshire Hathaway Ownership
points: Brooks Running, owned by Berkshire Hathaway since 2006 (acquired via Fruit of the Loom subsidiary, made standalone in 2012), has grown revenue 12% year-to-date in 2026 while rivals Nike and Under Armour struggle.
Year-to-date regional sales growth: 9% in Americas and Asia-Pacific, 24% in Europe, Middle East, and Africa.
Brooks holds the No. 1 market share position in US specialty running retail, led by its Ghost and Adrenaline GTS shoe models.

Berkshire's decentralized ownership model gives Brooks patient capital (capital invested without pressure for immediate returns) and operational autonomy, enabling 5-10 year strategic planning instead of quarterly earnings focus.
Brooks CEO Dan Sheridan calls Berkshire ownership 'a competitive advantage... in every market,' contrasting with the quarterly pressure facing competitors.
Warren Buffett stepped down as Berkshire chairman in September 2026, but his long-term capital allocation philosophy continues to underpin Brooks' performance.

issues.subject: Morning Brief: How Warren Buffett still looms over red-hot Brooks Running

headlines: Brooks Running, owned by Berkshire Hathaway since 2006, is thriving with 12% revenue growth year-to-date while Nike and Under Armour struggle, demonstrating Warren Buffett's patient capital strategy still works.
Berkshire's decentralized ownership model allowed Brooks to avoid discounting wars, innovate independently, and capture the No. 1 market share in US specialty running retail.
Brooks CEO Dan Sheridan credits Berkshire ownership as a competitive advantage, enabling long-term thinking in 5-10 year horizons rather than quarterly pressure.
Year-to-date through September, Brooks grew sales 9% in Americas and Asia-Pacific, and 24% in Europe, Middle East, and Africa regions.
Warren Buffett stepped down as Berkshire chairman in September but his acquisition and management philosophy continues to drive Brooks' red-hot performance.

sections.title: Brooks Running's Berkshire Advantage
points: 1. Berkshire acquired Brooks through Fruit of the Loom subsidiary in 2006, then elevated it to standalone subsidiary status in 2012 after recognizing its durable brand and market share gains.

2. The ownership model gives Brooks operational autonomy plus access to patient capital (capital deployed without pressure for immediate returns), allowing 5-10 year strategic planning instead of quarterly earnings focus.

3. Freedom from discounting wars and corporate synergy demands enabled Brooks to invest heavily in product innovation, resulting in recognition as having some of the best running sneakers available today.

4. CEO Dan Sheridan explicitly stated that Berkshire ownership is 'a competitive advantage for us in every market we go into' and contrasts sharply with the quarterly pressure facing competitors like Nike and Under Armour.

sections.title: Financial Performance and Market Position
points: 1. Brooks delivered 12% revenue growth through the first three quarters of 2026, with growth across all global regions.
2. Year-to-date sales growth: 9% increase in Americas and Asia-Pacific regions, 24% increase in Europe, Middle East, and Africa—demonstrating strong international expansion.
3. Brooks captured the No. 1 market share position in US specialty running retail with flagship products like the Ghost and Adrenaline GTS shoes.
4. Performance stands in stark contrast to struggling competitors: Nike and Under Armour are both facing significant headwinds while Brooks accelerates.
